title: Autoimmune Hepatitis
subject: Medicine
summary: Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic immune‑mediated liver inflammation presenting with jaundice, fatigue and elevated transaminases. Diagnosis relies on autoantibodies, IgG, and exclusion of other causes. Treatment is immunosuppression, monitoring for fibrosis and complications.

sections.p: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a progressive, immune‑driven hepatitis that can lead to cirrhosis if untreated. Diagnosis uses the International AIH Group criteria, combining clinical, serologic and histologic data.
b: International criteria score ≥15 (definite) or 10‑14 (probable).
Key serologies: ANA, ASMA, anti‑LKM1, anti‑LC1; IgG > upper‑limit of normal.
Liver biopsy shows interface hepatitis with plasma cell infiltrate.

sections.p: Severity is staged histologically (Scheuer or METAVIR) and by biochemical activity. Fibrosis stage guides prognosis and need for surveillance.
b: Activity grade (A0‑A3) reflects necro‑inflammatory severity.
Fibrosis stage (F0‑F4); F3‑F4 indicates advanced disease needing close follow‑up.

sections.p: AIH is idiopathic but associated with genetic predisposition (HLA‑DR3/DR4) and triggers common in low‑resource settings.
b: Genetic susceptibility (HLA‑DR3, DR4).
Infections that can precipitate AIH: hepatitis B/C, HIV, schistosomiasis, malaria.
Herbal or traditional medicines containing hepatotoxic compounds.
Concurrent autoimmune diseases (e.g., thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes).

sections.p: Patients often present with nonspecific symptoms; in East Africa, co‑existing infections may mask classic features.
b: Fatigue, anorexia, mild right‑upper‑quadrant discomfort.
Jaundice, dark urine, pruritus.
Elevated transaminases (ALT/AST >5× ULN) with relatively normal ALP.
Hypergammaglobulinemia (IgG).

sections.p: If a test is unavailable (e.g., anti‑LKM1), rely on available antibodies, IgG, and biopsy. Empiric steroid trial may be considered when suspicion is high and other causes are excluded.

t.b: Is there hepatocellular injury? – Markedly raised levels support AIH; if normal, look for cholestatic or vascular causes.
Is there immune activation? – IgG >1.1× ULN strengthens AIH diagnosis.
Which autoimmune pattern is present? – Positive ANA/ASMA suggests type 1; anti‑LKM1 suggests type 2.
Are there structural lesions or biliary obstruction? – Normal or mild fatty change supports AIH; gallstones suggest alternative diagnosis.
What is the histologic activity and fibrosis? – Interface hepatitis with plasma cells confirms AIH; fibrosis stage guides management.

t.a: Viral hepatitis serology (HBsAg, anti‑HBc, HCV RNA)
t.b: Is there a viral trigger? – Positive results require treating the infection first; AIH diagnosis only after exclusion.
Are co‑infections present? – Positive tests may influence immunosuppression choice.

sections.p: Complications arise from uncontrolled inflammation or treatment side effects.
b: Acute liver failure (INR >1.5, encephalopathy).
Progressive fibrosis → cirrhosis, portal hypertension.
Hepatocellular carcinoma risk increases when cirrhosis develops.
Steroid‑induced diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis.

sections.p: Goal: induce remission, prevent fibrosis, and manage complications. First‑line immunosuppression is steroids plus a steroid‑sparing agent.
b: If azathioprine intolerant, mycophenolate mofetil is an alternative – less hepatotoxic but more costly.
Avoid drugs that worsen liver injury (e.g., isoniazid in active TB, methotrexate).
Vaccinate against hepatitis A/B and pneumococcus before immunosuppression.

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects relapse, drug toxicity and progression.
b: Liver enzymes and IgG every 2‑4 weeks during induction, then every 3‑6 months.
CBC and renal function with azathioprine.
Ultrasound ± elastography annually after fibrosis stage ≥F2.
Bone density scan after 2 years of steroids.
Educate patients on avoiding hepatotoxic herbs and alcohol.

sections.p: Several liver diseases mimic AIH clinically and biochemically.
b: Viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV) – distinguished by viral markers.
Drug‑induced liver injury – history of offending drug, often eosinophilia.
Primary biliary cholangitis – cholestatic pattern, AMA positive.
Non‑alcoholic steatohepatitis – metabolic risk factors, steatosis on imaging.

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring or alarming.
b: Normal ALT in late disease – fibrosis may be present despite normal enzymes.
Low‑titer ANA in healthy individuals – must be interpreted with IgG and histology.
Transient rise in IgG after recent infection – repeat after 2 weeks.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening jaundice with INR >1.5 or encephalopathy (possible acute liver failure).
Severe abdominal pain with signs of peritonitis (possible rupture of varices).
Uncontrolled hypertension or hyperglycaemia after steroid initiation.

faq.q: Why is a liver biopsy still needed if autoantibodies are positive?
faq.a: Biopsy confirms interface hepatitis and assesses fibrosis, which guides treatment intensity.
Yes, though it is more common in women; presentation and management are the same.
Mycophenolate mofetil or calcineurin inhibitors can be used, but monitoring for infection is essential.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman from rural Kenya presents with fatigue, jaundice and ALT 800 U/L. Which investigations confirm AIH and why? — Order ANA/ASMA, IgG, viral serology, and biopsy; positive autoantibodies + high IgG + compatible histology confirm AIH after excluding hepatitis B/C.

During induction you notice rising blood pressure and blood glucose. How do you adjust therapy? — Add a steroid‑sparing agent (azathioprine) early and taper steroids; monitor BP and glucose, treat hypertension/diabetes concurrently.
A patient on azathioprine develops leukopenia. What is your next step? — Stop azathioprine, assess TPMT activity if available, and consider mycophenolate as alternative.

How do you differentiate AIH type 1 from type 2 in a child with elevated transaminases? — Type 1 shows ANA/ASMA positivity; type 2 shows anti‑LKM1 or anti‑LC1; age and severity differ, influencing prognosis.
What are the indications for liver transplantation in AIH? — Acute liver failure (INR >1.5, encephalopathy) or decompensated cirrhosis with refractory disease despite optimal immunosuppression.
Explain why a patient with co‑existing hepatitis B should receive antiviral therapy before steroids. — Steroids can reactivate HBV; antiviral prophylaxis prevents fulminant hepatitis.
Which non‑invasive test can monitor fibrosis when biopsy is not feasible? — Transient elastography; values >9.5 kPa suggest significant fibrosis (≥F2).

A patient reports using traditional herbal tea for malaria prophylaxis. How does this affect your management? — Some herbs are hepatotoxic and may trigger AIH; advise cessation and monitor liver enzymes closely.
